records.topic: The Trees That Blacked Out 55 Million People
records.coreQuestion: How did overgrown trees and a software bug black out 55 million people?
records.openingLine: Why overgrown trees blacked out 55 million people.
records.secondBeat: One August afternoon, sagging lines touched trees in Ohio.
records.dependency: Transmission lines depend on cleared rights-of-way so sagging conductors never touch vegetation.
records.mechanism: Hot, heavily loaded lines sag; if they touch trees, they trip and shift load onto neighbouring lines.
records.bottleneck: Tree trimming along thousands of kilometres of corridor is easy to defer.
records.failureConsequence: One line trips into a tree, others overload, and the grid cascades.
records.resilience: Reliability standards now mandate vegetation management and alarm monitoring.
records.expectedConsequence: a local fault cascades into a regional blackout
visualScenes: control room with a frozen alarm screen
night skyline of dark New York
editorialTitles: How Trees Helped Black Out 55 Million People
Why Grid Reliability Starts With Tree Trimming

facts.claim: The outage affected an estimated 55 million people, including 10 million people in southern and central Ontario and 45 million people in eight U.S. states.

The blackout was due to a software bug in the alarm system at the control room of FirstEnergy, which rendered operators unaware of the need to redistribute load after overloaded transmission lines dropped in voltage.
FirstEnergy failed to manage adequately tree growth in its transmission rights-of-way.
In the minutes before the event, the NYISO-managed power system was carrying 28,700 MW of load; at the height of the outage, the load had dropped to 5,716 MW, a loss of 80%.

narration.text: Why overgrown trees blacked out 55 million people.
One August afternoon, sagging lines touched trees in Ohio.
The utility had failed to manage tree growth along its lines.
A software bug froze the control room's alarms.
New York's load fell from 28,700 to 5,716 megawatts.
That's an 80% loss in minutes.
That's why grid reliability starts with a chainsaw.

records.topic: The Blackout That Dropped 31 GW in Seconds
records.coreQuestion: How did Spain and Portugal lose 31 gigawatts of load in seconds?
records.openingLine: Why Iberia lost 31 gigawatts in seconds.
records.secondBeat: One April day, Spain and Portugal's grid collapsed.
records.dependency: Grid stability depends on voltage control and spinning inertia from machines like synchronous condensers.
records.mechanism: Spinning machines resist sudden frequency and voltage changes, buying operators time to react.
records.bottleneck: Grids with less voltage-controlling capacity have less margin in a disturbance.
records.failureConsequence: Voltage runs out of control, generators trip, and the grid collapses.
records.resilience: Operators now schedule more voltage-controlling plant and add synchronous condensers.
records.expectedConsequence: a whole peninsula goes dark within seconds
editorialTitles: How Iberia's Grid Collapsed in Seconds
Why Grids Need Voltage Control, Not Just Power

facts.claim: The total disconnected load was 31 GW.
12:33:18 – 12:33:21 CEST – grid frequency of the Iberian Peninsula drops below 48.0 Hz.
By 07:00 CEST on 29 April, electricity had been restored to 99% of energy demand.
The Chair of the ENTSO-E Board stated: The problem is not renewable energy, but voltage control, regardless of the type of generation.

In the following days, gas turbines were delivering more power than usual, as their inertia and voltage stability was demanded by the grid operator, but increasing the cost by about 1 eurocent per kWh.

narration.text: Why Iberia lost 31 gigawatts in seconds.
One April day, Spain and Portugal's grid collapsed.
Frequency fell below 48.0 hertz in three seconds.
Europe's grid body blamed voltage control, not renewables.
Afterwards, gas turbines ran more for their inertia and voltage support.
Power was back to 99% of demand by the next morning.
That's why grids need machines that steady voltage, not just megawatts.

records.topic: The Anchor That Cut 75% of a Region's Traffic
records.coreQuestion: How can one dragged anchor cut a region off from the internet?
records.openingLine: Why cable breaks cut 75% of Mideast links.
records.secondBeat: In 2008, cable breaks hit links from the Middle East.
records.dependency: Internet traffic between the Middle East, Asia and Europe depends on a few submarine cable routes.
records.mechanism: Cables lie on the seabed near shore, where anchors and fishing gear can snag them.
records.bottleneck: Many cables share the same narrow routes near landing points.
records.failureConsequence: One incident can cut several cables at once.
records.resilience: Traffic reroutes through other cables, at lower capacity.
records.expectedConsequence: internet slows across whole countries until repairs
visualScenes: ship anchor dragging on the seabed
traffic map Middle East to Europe
editorialTitles: How One Anchor Cut the Internet
Why Cable Protection Zones Matter

facts.claim: The 2008 submarine cable disruption refers to three separate incidents of major damage to submarine optical communication cables around the world.
The break disrupted 75% of communication between the Middle East and Asia and the rest of the world.
This cut was caused by an abandoned anchor weighing 5-6 tonnes.
1.7 million Internet users in the UAE were affected by the Internet disruption.

narration.text: Why cable breaks cut 75% of Mideast links.
In 2008, cable breaks hit links from the Middle East.
75% of its communication with the wider world was disrupted.
One cut came from an abandoned anchor of 5 to 6 tonnes.
1.7 million internet users in the UAE felt it.
Cables crowd into the same shallow routes near shore.
That's why the internet's weakest point is where cables reach land.

records.topic: The Earthquake That Cut Asia's Internet
records.coreQuestion: How did one earthquake off Taiwan disrupt internet and phone service across Asia?
records.openingLine: Why two earthquakes cut Asia's calls to 40%.
records.secondBeat: In 2006, shocks of 7.0 and 6.9 struck off Taiwan.
records.dependency: Asia's international telecoms depend on submarine cables crossing a seismically active region.
records.mechanism: Earthquake-triggered undersea slides sever cables; repair ships must locate and splice each break.
records.bottleneck: Few repair ships serve the region, and each break takes days to fix.
records.failureConsequence: Several cables failing together cut capacity sharply for weeks.
records.resilience: Traffic reroutes over surviving cables and satellites at reduced capacity.
records.expectedConsequence: calls and internet slow for weeks during repairs
editorialTitles: The Earthquake That Cut Asia's Internet
Why Finding a Cable Break Takes So Long

facts.claim: The International Seismological Centre measured the shocks at 7.0 and 6.9 on the moment magnitude scale.
Several submarine communications cables were cut, disrupting telecommunication services in various parts of Asia.
The international calling capacity was reduced to 40%.
It was estimated that the first part of the repair of one of the submarine cables would be completed around 16 January 2007.
Internet services had resumed to 70% of normal levels.

narration.text: Why two earthquakes cut Asia's calls to 40%.
In 2006, shocks of 7.0 and 6.9 struck off Taiwan.
Several submarine cables were cut at once.
International calling capacity fell to 40%.
Repair ships had to find and splice each break.
The first repairs weren't expected until mid-January 2007.
That's why cable resilience depends on the repair fleet.

records.topic: The Satellite System That Rescued 63,745 People
records.coreQuestion: How does a distress beacon at sea reach rescuers anywhere on Earth?
records.openingLine: Why 63,745 people owe their rescue to satellites.
records.secondBeat: Cospas-Sarsat has relayed distress alerts since 1982.
records.dependency: Ships, aircraft and hikers depend on satellite detection of 406 MHz distress beacons.
records.mechanism: Satellites detect beacon signals, locate them and forward alerts to rescue centres.
records.bottleneck: Only 406 MHz digital beacons are monitored by satellite.
records.failureConsequence: Old 121.5 MHz beacons rely on nearby aircraft and can go unheard.
records.resilience: Multiple satellite constellations carry the search-and-rescue payload.
records.expectedConsequence: rescues slow when beacons can't be detected
visualScenes: distress beacon activating on a life raft
editorialTitles: The Satellites That Hear a Call for Help
How Cospas-Sarsat Rescued Thousands

facts.claim: Between September 1982 and December 2023 the Cospas-Sarsat System provided assistance in rescuing at least 63,745 people in 19,883 SAR events.
Distress alerts are detected, located and forwarded to over 200 countries and territories at no cost to beacon owners or the receiving government agencies.
Cospas-Sarsat only monitors for alerts from digital distress beacons that transmit on 406 MHz.
Older beacons that transmit using the legacy analog signal on 121.5 MHz or 243 MHz rely on being received only by nearby aircraft or rescue personnel.

narration.text: Why 63,745 people owe their rescue to satellites.
Cospas-Sarsat has relayed distress alerts since 1982.
Alerts go to over 200 countries and territories, free.
Satellites only listen for 406-megahertz digital beacons.
Old 121.5-megahertz beacons rely on a nearby plane hearing them.
That's 19,883 search-and-rescue events so far.
That's why a beacon's frequency can decide whether help comes.

records.topic: The Tunnel Fire That Closed the Alps for 3 Years
records.coreQuestion: How did one truck fire close a key Alpine tunnel for three years?
records.openingLine: A truck fire shut Mont Blanc until 2002.
records.secondBeat: The 1999 blaze started in a single truck.
records.dependency: Road freight between France and Italy depends on the Mont Blanc Tunnel.
records.mechanism: Ventilation and fire systems must clear smoke and heat fast in a long, single-bore tunnel.
records.bottleneck: A single tube with split management left little margin in a fire.
records.failureConsequence: Smoke and heat trapped drivers; the tunnel stayed shut for years.
records.resilience: Unified management, shelters and truck spacing rules followed.
records.expectedConsequence: freight detours across other Alpine routes
editorialTitles: The Fire That Closed the Mont Blanc Tunnel
Why Tunnel Ventilation Is Life or Death

facts.claim: On the morning of 24 March 1999, the engine of a Belgian transport truck carrying volatile freight caught fire in the tunnel.
The event expanded into a catastrophe which killed 39 people.
The fire led to a tunnel closure until 9 March 2002.
It reduces the route from France to Turin by 50 kilometres (30 miles) and to Milan by 100 km (60 mi).
The tunnel is 11.611 km (7.215 mi) in length, 8.6 m (28 ft) in width, and 4.35 m (14.3 ft) in height.
Within the tunnel, a minimum speed of 50 km/h and a maximum speed of 70 km/h applies, while the prescribed distance between vehicles is 150 m.

narration.text: A truck fire shut Mont Blanc until 2002.
The 1999 blaze started in a single truck.
39 people died.
The tunnel stayed closed until March 2002.
It's 11.611 kilometres long, in a single tube.
It cuts the drive from France to Milan by 100 kilometres.
Vehicles must now keep 150 metres apart.
That's why a tunnel's ventilation matters as much as its length.

records.topic: The Dose That Ended Typhoid in Tap Water
records.coreQuestion: How did adding a trace of chlorine transform public health?
records.openingLine: Why 0.2 parts per million changed public health.
records.secondBeat: That's roughly the chlorine dose early systems used.
records.dependency: Safe drinking water depends on continuous disinfection at treatment plants.
records.mechanism: Small, controlled chlorine doses kill pathogens that cause cholera, dysentery and typhoid.
records.bottleneck: Dosing must be continuous and correctly calibrated.
records.failureConsequence: If dosing lapses, waterborne disease can return quickly.
records.resilience: Monitoring, backup dosing and alternative disinfectants add layers.
records.expectedConsequence: boil-water notices follow any dosing failure
editorialTitles: The Tiny Dose That Made Tap Water Safe
Why Chlorination Changed Public Health

facts.claim: Permanent water chlorination began in 1905, when a faulty slow sand filter and a contaminated water supply caused a serious typhoid fever epidemic in Lincoln, England.
The first continuous use of chlorine in the United States for disinfection took place in 1908 at Boonton Reservoir, which served as the supply for Jersey City, New Jersey.
Chlorination was achieved by controlled additions of dilute solutions of chloride of lime (calcium hypochlorite) at doses of 0.2 to 0.35 ppm.
In a paper published in 1894, it was formally proposed to add chlorine to water to render it germ-free.
Chlorination is used to prevent the spread of waterborne diseases such as cholera, dysentery, and typhoid.
In 1897, the town of Maidstone, England, was the first to have its entire water supply treated with chlorine.

narration.text: Why 0.2 parts per million changed public health.
That's roughly the chlorine dose early systems used.
In 1897, Maidstone treated its whole supply.
Chlorine was first proposed for drinking water in 1894.
In 1905, a typhoid outbreak made Lincoln chlorinate permanently.
By 1908, Jersey City had continuous disinfection.
If dosing stops, waterborne disease can return fast.
That's why a small pump is one of medicine's biggest wins.

records.topic: The Carton That Lets Milk Skip the Fridge
records.coreQuestion: How can milk sit on a shelf for months without refrigeration?
records.openingLine: Why 1 sterile machine replaced the milk fridge.
records.secondBeat: Aseptic packaging removed the need for a cold chain.
records.dependency: Shelf-stable milk and juice depend on aseptic filling of sterile product into sterile cartons.
records.mechanism: Product and packaging are sterilised separately, then filled and sealed in a sterile zone.
records.bottleneck: A few specialised machine makers supply most aseptic filling lines.
records.failureConsequence: A contaminated or stopped line halts shelf-stable output.
records.resilience: Chilled distribution can replace some volume, at higher cost.
records.expectedConsequence: shelf-stable supply tightens and cold-chain costs rise
visualScenes: distribution truck in a hot region
editorialTitles: How Milk Survives Without a Fridge
The Machine That Replaced the Cold Chain

facts.claim: In the 1960s and 1970s, the development of the Tetra Brik package and the aseptic packaging technology made supply possible without the need for a cold chain.
In 1952, the first filling machine producing 100 ml cream tetrahedrons was delivered to a local dairy.
In 1954, the first machine producing 500 ml milk packages was sold to a Stockholm dairy.
Tetra Pak's commercial breakthrough arrived in the mid-1960s with the Tetra Brik package, introduced in 1963, and the development of the aseptic technology.
In 1964, the first Tetra Classic Aseptic machine outside of Europe was installed in Lebanon.

narration.text: Why 1 sterile machine replaced the milk fridge.
Aseptic packaging removed the need for a cold chain.
Product and carton are sterilised, then sealed together.
The first filling machine, in 1952, made 100 ml cream packs.
The Tetra Brik arrived in 1963.
If a sterile line fails, shelf-stable output stops.
That's why a filling machine can replace a refrigerator.

records.topic: The Wheat Fungus That Spread Across 3 Continents
records.coreQuestion: How did one wheat fungus spread from Uganda to Iran, and why does surveillance matter?
records.openingLine: Why one fungus can destroy 100% of wheat.
records.secondBeat: Ug99 stem rust was found in Uganda in 1999.
records.dependency: Wheat harvests depend on surveillance that spots new rust strains before they spread.
records.mechanism: Fungal spores travel on wind; surveillance networks track new races and guide resistant varieties.
records.bottleneck: Ug99 overcame resistance genes that had protected wheat for decades.
records.failureConsequence: Without early detection, susceptible wheat can lose up to 100% of its crop.
records.resilience: Breeders deploy new resistance genes, guided by surveillance data.
records.expectedConsequence: wheat losses spread before resistant seed can be planted
editorialTitles: The Fungus That Threatens the World's Wheat
Why Crop Disease Surveillance Matters

facts.claim: Ug99 can cause up to 100% crop losses and is virulent against many resistance genes which have previously protected wheat against stem rust.
It was found in Uganda in 1999, Kenya in 2001, Ethiopia in 2003, Sudan and Yemen in 2006, Iran in 2007, and Tanzania in 2009, Eritrea in 2012, and Rwanda and Egypt in 2014.
These resistant Sr genes, of which 50 are known, give wheat different resistances to stem rust.
Like most Ug99 races, and unlike other stem rust varieties, it is virulent against the Sr gene Sr31.

narration.text: Why one fungus can destroy 100% of wheat.
Ug99 stem rust was found in Uganda in 1999.
By 2007, it had spread as far as Iran.
It beat resistance genes that had protected wheat for decades.
About 50 resistance genes are known.
Surveillance tells breeders which ones still work.
That's why bread depends on people tracking spores.

records.topic: The 1 Million Beehives Trucked to California
records.coreQuestion: Why do beekeepers from almost every U.S. state truck their hives to California each spring?
records.openingLine: Why 1 million beehives travel to California.
records.secondBeat: It's the world's largest managed pollination event.
records.dependency: California's almond crop depends on hives trucked in by migratory beekeepers.
records.mechanism: Pollination brokers contract hives from across the country for a few weeks of bloom.
records.bottleneck: Nearly half of U.S. hives must be in one valley at once.
records.failureConsequence: Colony losses or transport disruption would cut almond yields.
records.resilience: Self-pollinating varieties reduce dependence on bees.
records.expectedConsequence: almond prices rise when hives run short
visualScenes: trucks loaded with beehives at night
map of hives converging on California
editorialTitles: The Biggest Pollination Event on Earth
Why Almonds Depend on Trucked-In Bees

facts.claim: The pollination of California's almonds is the largest annual managed pollination event in the world, with over 1 million hives (nearly half of all beehives in the U.S.) being brought to the almond groves.
California produces about 80% of the world's almond supply.
Much of the supply of bees is managed by pollination brokers, who contract with migratory beekeepers from at least 49 states for the event.
Due to high acreage and water demand for almond cultivation, and need for pesticides, California almond production may be unsustainable.

narration.text: Why 1 million beehives travel to California.
It's the world's largest managed pollination event.
That's nearly half of all beehives in the U.S.
California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
Brokers bring in beekeepers from at least 49 states.
A bad year for bees means a bad year for almonds.
That's why a nut harvest depends on trucks full of bees.

records.coreQuestion: How did a computer worm physically damage industrial machines?
records.secondBeat: Stuxnet surfaced in 2010 after years of development.
records.dependency: Factories, pipelines and power plants depend on programmable logic controllers to run physical equipment.
records.mechanism: PLCs execute control logic; if their programming is subverted, machines can be driven to damage themselves.
records.bottleneck: PLC programming tools run on ordinary PCs that malware can reach.
records.failureConsequence: Compromised controllers can wreck equipment while reporting normal operation.
records.resilience: Network segmentation and code signing make PLC tampering harder.
records.expectedConsequence: physical damage hidden behind normal-looking readouts
editorialTitles: The Worm That Broke Machines
Why PLCs Are Cyber Targets

facts.claim: Stuxnet is a malicious computer worm first uncovered on 17 June 2010 and thought to have been in development since at least 2005.
Targeting industrial control systems, the worm infected over 200,000 computers and caused 1,000 machines to physically degrade.
Exploiting four zero-day flaws in the systems, Stuxnet functions by targeting machines using the Microsoft Windows operating system and networks, then seeking out Siemens Step7 software.
Stuxnet infects PLCs by subverting the Step-7 software application that is used to reprogram these devices.

narration.text: Why one worm broke 1,000 machines.
Stuxnet surfaced in 2010 after years of development.
It infected over 200,000 computers.
It used four zero-day flaws to reach Siemens Step 7 software.
It reached them through ordinary Windows PCs.
Then it reprogrammed the controllers running physical machines.
The machines degraded while operators saw little wrong.
That's why factory controllers are now security targets.

records.topic: The Certificate Authority That Collapsed in Months
records.coreQuestion: What happens when a company that vouches for websites gets hacked?
records.openingLine: Why 500 fake certificates killed a company.
records.dependency: Secure web connections depend on certificate authorities that browsers trust.
records.mechanism: Browsers trust certificates signed by approved authorities; a compromised authority can sign fakes.
records.bottleneck: One compromised authority can vouch for any website.
records.failureConsequence: Fake certificates enable man-in-the-middle attacks on users.
records.resilience: Browsers can distrust an authority entirely; certificate logs now detect fakes.
records.expectedConsequence: the authority's certificates are revoked and the company fails
editorialTitles: The Hack That Broke Web Trust
Why One Certificate Authority Can Endanger Millions

facts.claim: DigiNotar BV was a Dutch certificate authority from 1998 to 2011.
The company was hacked in June 2011 and it issued hundreds of fraudulent certificates, some of which were used for man-in-the-middle attacks on Iranian Gmail users.
After more than 500 fake DigiNotar certificates were found, major web browser makers reacted by blacklisting all DigiNotar certificates.
On 10 January 2011 the company was sold to VASCO Data Security International.
It was acquired in January 2011 by VASCO and subsequently declared bankrupt in September of the same year.

narration.text: Why 500 fake certificates killed a company.
DigiNotar vouched for websites from 1998.
Browsers trust any certificate a trusted authority signs.
In June 2011, it was hacked.
Fake certificates were used to spy on Iranian Gmail users.
Browsers then blacklisted every DigiNotar certificate.
By September 2011, the company was bankrupt.
That's why web trust rests on a few signing keys.

records.topic: The Contaminated Ingredient That Killed 81 People
records.coreQuestion: How did a contaminated drug ingredient from overseas kill patients in U.S. hospitals?
records.openingLine: Why one contaminated ingredient killed 81 people.
records.secondBeat: In 2008, adulterated heparin reached U.S. patients.
records.dependency: Finished medicines depend on active ingredients often made by distant suppliers.
records.mechanism: Ingredient makers must qualify their own suppliers; contamination upstream passes into finished drugs.
records.bottleneck: Long supply chains make it hard to verify every upstream source.
records.failureConsequence: An adulterated ingredient reaches patients as a trusted brand-name drug.
records.resilience: Supplier audits, testing and international guidelines tighten oversight.
visualScenes: supply chain map from raw material to hospital
editorialTitles: The Drug Ingredient That Poisoned a Supply Chain
Why Medicine Depends on Distant Suppliers

facts.claim: 2008 Chinese heparin adulteration refers to heparin adulteration incidents that occurred in the United States of America in 2008.
Baxter then sold this adulterated heparin in the US, which killed 81 people, and left 785 severely injured.
According to the internationally harmonized guideline, ICH Q7, API manufacturers are fully responsible for qualifying their suppliers through on-site audits, testing, and regular communications.
The heparin incidents occurred in 2008.

narration.text: Why one contaminated ingredient killed 81 people.
In 2008, adulterated heparin reached U.S. patients.
It also left 785 people severely injured.
The ingredient passed through a long supply chain first.
Guidelines now make ingredient makers audit their suppliers.
One bad source upstream can reach every hospital downstream.
That's why drug safety starts far before the pharmacy.

records.topic: The Outage That Grounded Every U.S. Departure
records.coreQuestion: How did one failed notice system ground every departure in the U.S.?
records.openingLine: Why one outage stopped every U.S. departure.
records.secondBeat: In January 2023, the FAA's NOTAM system went offline.
records.dependency: Pilots depend on NOTAMs, notices about runway closures and hazards, before every flight.
records.mechanism: The NOTAM system distributes safety notices that crews must review before departure.
records.bottleneck: One central system feeds notices to all flights.
records.failureConsequence: When it went offline, the FAA paused all domestic departures.
records.resilience: Backup systems and manual procedures restored service within hours.
records.expectedConsequence: a nationwide ground stop and a day of delays
editorialTitles: The Notice System That Grounded America
Why One FAA Outage Stopped Every Flight

facts.claim: On January 11, the FAA ordered airlines to pause all domestic departures after its pilot-alerting Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system went offline overnight, causing extensive disruption.
The outage was the first time since September 11, 2001, that the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop in the United States.
Flights were beginning to resume departures after the FAA terminated the NOTAM outage advisory, and departures at other airports were expected to resume by 9 am.
Southwest Airlines was down 2.4%, while Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines were down about 1%.

narration.text: Why one outage stopped every U.S. departure.
In January 2023, the FAA's NOTAM system went offline.
NOTAMs warn pilots about closed runways and hazards.
The FAA paused all domestic departures.
It was the first nationwide ground stop since 2001.
Flights began resuming later that morning.
One central notice system fed every flight.
That's why aviation safety depends on unglamorous databases.

records.topic: The Radio Backup to GPS That Was Switched Off
records.coreQuestion: Why did the U.S. turn off its radio navigation backup, and why do people want it back?
records.openingLine: Why America switched off its GPS backup.
records.secondBeat: Loran-C's U.S. stations went dark in 2010.
records.dependency: Navigation and timing users depend on GPS, with few terrestrial backups.
records.mechanism: Loran stations broadcast powerful low-frequency pulses that receivers time to fix position.
records.bottleneck: Once shut down, the network can't simply be switched back on.
records.failureConsequence: Without a terrestrial backup, GPS jamming leaves users with fewer options.
records.resilience: Proposals for eLoran would restore a hard-to-jam timing signal.
records.expectedConsequence: GPS outages bite harder without a fallback
editorialTitles: The GPS Backup America Switched Off
Why eLoran Keeps Coming Back

facts.claim: In 2010, the US and Canadian systems were shut down, along with Loran-C/CHAYKA stations that were shared with Russia.
At the end of 2015, navigation chains in most of Europe were turned off.
This process eventually settled on the band from 90 to 100 kHz.
In December 2015 there was renewed discussion of funding an eLoran system, and NIST offered to fund development of a microchip-sized eLoran receiver for distribution of timing signals.
Loran-C was used primarily by militaries after it was introduced in 1957.

narration.text: Why America switched off its GPS backup.
Loran-C's U.S. stations went dark in 2010.
It used the band from 90 to 100 kilohertz.
Most European chains went dark at the end of 2015.
That same year, talk of a modern eLoran revived.
Towers torn down can't be switched back on.
That's why GPS's biggest weakness is having no understudy.
